sections.content: How many people stayed in Maidstone after gaining qualifications?

Maidstone is a large town in the South East. Maidstone does not have its own university.

Maidstone has medium levels of deprivation.

Overall, Maidstone ended up with:

  • fewer graduates than it produced
  • a similar number of non-graduates with advanced qualifications as it produced
Note: all towns and cities in this analysis are defined based on population size only. This means that some cities are classed as towns because of their population.

Let's explore this further

There were 4,665 state-school pupils from Maidstone who sat their GCSEs between the 2007 to 2008 and the 2010 to 2011 school years.

Of these, 1,630 (35%) went on to gain degree-level qualifications (level 6+ as defined by The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation, or Ofqual ). We will call these people graduates.

Another 1,295 (28%) went on to gain other advanced post-16 qualifications, such as A-Levels, a foundation degree or higher apprenticeship (levels 3-5 as defined by Ofqual). In this tool, we will refer to these non-graduates with advanced qualifications as “qualified non-graduates", for brevity.

The charts below compare Maidstone to other English towns and cities using three measures:

  • what proportion of Maidstone's pupils became graduates or qualified non-graduates by the 2017 to 2018 academic year
  • of those graduates and qualified non-graduates, the percentages that lived in Maidstone in the 2018 to 2019 academic year
  • how many graduates and qualified non-graduates from elsewhere came to live there by 2018 to 2019, relative to the number who sat their GCSEs there

In some towns, some of this information may not be available because of small sample sizes.
The size and deprivation level of a town, as well as the qualification levels of older residents, were all related to students' educational attainment. Read our previous analysis.

Where did those who left Maidstone move to?

Of Maidstone's graduates, 655 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 105 of those graduates (16%) were living fairly locally, in the Medway travel to work area (TTWA).

Of Maidstone's qualified (level 3+) non-graduates, 325 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 145 of those qualified non-graduates (45%) were living fairly locally, in the Medway travel to work area (TTWA).

Of those in Maidstone's GCSE cohort:

  • 390 graduates left the South East
  • the most common region they moved to was London
  • 105 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates left the South East
  • the most common region they moved to was London

In 2018 to 2019, 30% of graduates and 33% of qualified non-graduates living in Maidstone had moved there from elsewhere

In the 2018 to 2019 academic year, there were 1,380 graduates and 1,405 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates from our cohort living in Maidstone. This is compared with the 1,630 graduates and 1,295 qualified non-graduates who had lived there when they sat their GCSEs.

In 2018 to 2019, 69% of the graduates had also lived in Maidstone as GCSE pupils, while 30% had moved there from elsewhere.

Of the qualified non-graduates who lived in Maidstone in 2018 to 2019, 68% had lived there as GCSE pupils, while 33% had moved to the area from elsewhere.
